title: Academic Reading: overall strategy
summary: 3 passages, 40 questions, 60 minutes with no extra transfer time. The passages get harder, so manage your time and never leave a blank.
rule: 60 minutes, no transfer time: about 20 minutes per passage, no blanks.

do: Skim 2–3 min: title, first sentences, names, dates
Read instructions: word limit and answer form
Underline key words, scan for synonyms
Do in-order tasks first, matching tasks last
avoid: 30 min on Passage 1 → rushed Passage 3
Options that repeat the passage's exact words
Your own knowledge instead of the passage
remember: Split time ~17 / 20 / 23 min; no transfer time
No penalty for wrong answers → guess every blank

steps: Split the hour as about 17 / 20 / 23 minutes for Passages 1 / 2 / 3. Passage 3 is the hardest and usually has more inference questions.
Skim the passage for 2–3 minutes: title, subtitle, the first sentence of each paragraph, names, dates and numbers. Write a 1–3 word note next to each paragraph.
Read the instructions for each question group: the word limit, the answer form (letters, words, Y/N/NG) and whether options can be used more than once.
Underline the key words in each question, especially names, numbers and capitalised words that cannot be paraphrased. Then scan for them or their synonyms.
Read the sentence before and after the place you find carefully, then answer. Most question groups follow the order of the passage.
Do the in-order tasks first (completion, TFNG, MCQ). Do the 'any order' tasks (matching information, matching features) last, when you already know the text.
With 1–2 minutes left for a passage, guess every empty answer and move on.
traps: Spending 30+ minutes on Passage 1 and rushing Passage 3. Set a checkpoint: Passage 2 should start by minute 17–20.
Word matching: the option or sentence that repeats the passage's exact words is often the distractor. The real answer is usually a paraphrase.
Using your own knowledge instead of what the passage actually says.
On paper: forgetting that there is NO transfer time in Reading. Write answers on the answer sheet as you go.
tips: Wrong answers lose no marks, so never leave a blank.
Copied words must be spelled exactly as in the passage. British or American spelling is fine, but a misspelled word is wrong.
Respect the word limit: 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS' means one or two words. A hyphenated word counts as one word, and a number in digits counts as a number.
For TFNG / YNNG write the form the instructions ask for. Writing TRUE in a YES/NO/NOT GIVEN task is marked wrong.
Rough targets: 30/40 ≈ band 7.0, 27 ≈ 6.5, 23 ≈ 6.0. Aim for 1.5 minutes per question.
Computer test: use the highlight and notes tools on key words (the app's reading screen also supports highlighting).
After a test, check every mistake against an explanation (the teacher used ieltsdeal.com): find the proving sentence and note the paraphrase you missed.
example: Illustrative: Question key word 'elderly' → in the passage look for 'older people' / 'pensioners' / 'over 65', not the word 'elderly' itself.
language: Paraphrase pairs: rose ↔ increased / climbed; not compulsory ↔ optional; cheap ↔ inexpensive / low-cost; began ↔ originated / dates back to
Limiting words to notice: only, all, always, never, most, some, the first, mainly

title: True / False / Not Given
summary: Decide whether each statement agrees with the FACTS in the passage, contradicts them, or is not covered.
rule: FALSE = the passage says the opposite; NOT GIVEN = it says nothing about it.

do: Underline key words + qualifiers (all, only, most)
Find the place; answers follow passage order
Compare the statement idea by idea
F or NG? A sentence makes it impossible → F
avoid: 'Some / many' does not confirm 'all / most'
A comparison the passage never makes → NG
Real-world knowledge: not in the passage → NG
remember: Write TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN, never YES / NO

steps: Read the statement and underline the key words plus any qualifier (all, only, always, more than, first, most).
Scan for the part of the passage that covers this topic. The answers follow passage order, so Q5 is between Q4 and Q6.
Read that sentence (and the ones around it) carefully and compare it with the statement idea by idea.
TRUE = the passage says the same thing in other words. FALSE = the passage says the opposite (a direct contradiction). NOT GIVEN = the passage gives no information about this specific claim.
If you are choosing between FALSE and NOT GIVEN, ask: 'Can I point to a sentence that makes this statement impossible?' If yes, FALSE. If not, NOT GIVEN.
traps: Qualifiers: a passage saying 'many' or 'some' does not confirm 'all' or 'most'. 'One of the first' is not 'the first'.
Comparisons: the statement says X is bigger / older / more popular, but the passage mentions both and never compares them → NOT GIVEN.
Partial match: the topic is in the passage but one detail (a reason, a date, a cause) is not → NOT GIVEN.
Using your own knowledge: even if the statement is true in real life, if the passage doesn't say it, it is NOT GIVEN.
Same words, different meaning: the statement reuses passage words but changes the subject, time or degree.
tips: Never write YES / NO here. Use TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN (or T / F / NG if allowed).
If you can't find the information quickly, it is often NOT GIVEN. Mark it, move on, and come back if time allows.
Usually there is at least one of each answer in a set, but don't rely on that pattern.
example: Statement: 'Children must go to the school where they are registered.' Passage: 'The law says that parents must ensure that their child regularly attends the school where he/she is registered.' must go ↔ must ensure … attends → TRUE.
language: Contradiction signals (often FALSE): however, in fact, contrary to, rather than, not until, no longer, it was later shown
Hedging that changes the claim: may, might, is thought to, it is possible that, some experts suggest

title: Yes / No / Not Given
summary: Decide whether each statement agrees with the WRITER'S views or claims, contradicts them, or is not covered.
rule: YES / NO = the writer's own view; no view on this exact point = NOT GIVEN.

do: Underline the opinion words and qualifiers
Find the paragraph; answers follow passage order
Separate the writer's view from reported views
Agrees = YES, disagrees = NO, no opinion = NG
avoid: 'Critics claim X' ≠ the writer believes X
'One factor' ≠ 'the main reason'
A fact mentioned ≠ the writer's opinion
remember: Write YES / NO / NOT GIVEN, never TRUE / FALSE

steps: Underline the opinion part of the statement (should, is wrong to, is the best way, is overrated) and any qualifier.
Find the paragraph where the writer discusses this point. The answers follow passage order.
Separate the writer's own view from the views the writer only reports ('Some critics argue…', 'It is widely believed…').
YES = the writer agrees. NO = the writer clearly disagrees or says the opposite. NOT GIVEN = the writer gives no opinion on this exact point.
traps: Reported views: 'Many people claim X' does not mean the writer believes X. Look for the writer's own reaction (however, but, this is mistaken).
Degree: the writer thinks something is 'one factor', while the statement says it is 'the main reason'.
A fact being mentioned does not mean the writer has an opinion about it.
Writing TRUE / FALSE instead of YES / NO is marked wrong.
tips: Use the exact form the instructions ask for: YES / NO / NOT GIVEN (the course answer keys use Y / N / NG).
This task appears most often with Passage 3 argument texts. Read the first and last paragraphs to get the writer's overall position.
example: Statement: 'Forsythe's findings contradicted previous beliefs on the function of fractals in art.' The passage describes fractals in art and Forsythe's work, but never says his findings contradicted earlier beliefs → NOT GIVEN.
language: Writer's stance: I would argue, it is clear that, undoubtedly, admittedly, surely, it is a mistake to, this is unconvincing
Reported (not the writer's) views: critics claim, it is often said, according to, some believe

title: Matching headings
summary: Choose the heading that summarises the MAIN IDEA of each paragraph or section. There are more headings than paragraphs.
rule: Match the heading to the whole paragraph's main idea, not to one detail.

do: Read all headings; underline each key idea
Cross out the heading used in the example
Read first 1–2 and last sentence → main idea
Do easy paragraphs first, cross off used ones
avoid: A heading that repeats a word from the paragraph
A heading that fits only one detail
Similar headings: 'causes' vs 'effects'
remember: Not in order; each heading used once
Do this task first: it maps the text

steps: Read all the headings first and underline the key idea in each (e.g. 'reasons for…', 'a failed attempt', 'future applications').
Cross out any heading used in the example.
For each paragraph, read the first one or two sentences and the last sentence, and decide its main idea in your own words.
Choose the heading that matches that main idea. Then read the whole paragraph quickly to confirm it covers the paragraph, not one sentence.
Do the easy paragraphs first. Cross out used headings, then decide the difficult ones from what is left.
traps: Word-matching trap: a heading that repeats a word from the paragraph is often wrong. Match the meaning, not the vocabulary.
Detail vs main idea: a heading that fits one example or detail in the paragraph is not the answer.
Two similar headings: check the exact focus, e.g. 'causes of' vs 'effects of', 'past' vs 'current'.
The topic sentence is not always first. A paragraph can start with background and turn at 'However…'.
tips: Do this task before the other questions on the passage. It gives you a map of the text.
Each heading is normally used only once.
Answers are not in order. Write the roman numerals carefully (iv ≠ vi).
example: Illustrative: A paragraph explains how researchers finally identified who built the moai statues. The heading 'ii' (a definite answer about the statues' origin) matches the main idea, while a heading about statue size only matches one detail.
language: Turn signals where the main idea often appears: however, but, yet, in fact, the key point is
Paragraph-function words in headings: reasons, consequences, comparison, a solution, a challenge, a turning point, an unexpected finding

title: Matching information (which paragraph contains…)
summary: Find which paragraph contains a specific piece of information, such as an example, a reason, a comparison or a reference to something.
rule: Find the paragraph with that exact TYPE of info: example, reason, figure…

do: Check: can a letter be used more than once?
Underline the info type + the topic
Do this task last, after the others
Scan likely paragraphs for a paraphrase
avoid: Expecting passage order: answers are random
Reading for main ideas: it's often one sentence
Topic is there, but not the type asked for

steps: Read the instructions: can a letter be used more than once? (Often 'NB You may use any letter more than once'.)
Underline the TYPE of information (an example of, a description of, a reason for, a comparison between, a reference to) and the topic.
Leave this task until after the other tasks on the passage, so you already know roughly where things are.
Use your paragraph notes to guess the likely paragraph, then scan it for a paraphrase of the topic and check that the type matches (for example, it really is an example, not a definition).
Answer the easiest ones first, guess the rest.
traps: Answers are NOT in passage order, and some paragraphs may have no answer.
The detail is often one sentence in the middle of a paragraph, not its main idea. Don't use heading-style reading here.
A paragraph can mention the topic without giving the requested type (it mentions costs but gives no 'estimate of costs').
tips: Watch for specific words in the question: 'a figure / statistic' → look for numbers; 'a named person' → look for names; 'a historical reference' → look for dates.
This is one of the most frequent reading tasks in the practice tests. Train scanning for paraphrases.
example: Illustrative: 'a reference to the cost of a project' → look for figures with $ / million, or words like expense, budget, funding.
language: Type words: example (for instance, such as), reason (because, due to, as a result of), comparison (whereas, unlike, compared with), prediction (will, is likely to, in future)

title: Matching features (people / theories / places / dates)
summary: Match statements or findings to the person, group, place or time they belong to.
rule: Match each statement to the person whose words say the same thing.

do: Highlight every name in the passage first
Read what each person found or claimed
Underline each statement's key idea, then match
Check: options may be reused or not used
avoid: Expecting passage order: statements are random
Missing later mentions (surname, he / she)
Choosing a nearby name, not who made the claim

steps: Look at the list of features (usually names) and find and highlight each one in the passage. Note that a name can appear more than once.
Read what the passage says next to each name: their finding, claim or opinion.
Read each statement, underline its key idea, and match it to the person whose words say the same thing in other words.
Check the instructions: options may be used more than once, and some may not be used.
traps: Statements are in random order, not in passage order.
Surnames only: after the first mention, a person is usually referred to by surname or by 'he / she / the researcher'. Follow the pronouns.
Two people discussing the same topic: check who actually made the claim, not who is mentioned nearby.
tips: Highlighting all the names first saves a lot of time.
If one person appears in only one place, match those statements first. It narrows down the rest.
example: Illustrative: Statement: 'Animal behaviour can be affected by artificial light.' Find the researcher who says that 'street lighting disrupts the patterns of nocturnal species'. That is the paraphrase.
language: Reporting verbs: argues, claims, suggests, found, demonstrated, proposed, questioned, rejected

title: Matching sentence endings
summary: Join each sentence beginning to the ending that makes a grammatical sentence that is TRUE according to the passage.
rule: The ending must fit the grammar AND say what the passage says.

do: Underline key words in each beginning
Find each beginning in the passage, in order
Predict the ending, then find the same meaning
Check grammar: singular/plural, verb form
avoid: Endings that fit grammatically but not the text
Extra endings that link to the wrong subject
Endings true in general, not in the passage
remember: Each ending used once; beginnings in order

steps: Read the sentence beginnings and underline their key words. They follow passage order.
Scan the passage for each beginning and read what the passage says about it.
Predict the ending in your own words, then find the option with the same meaning.
Check the grammar: does the ending fit the beginning (singular/plural, verb form, a clause vs a noun phrase)?
traps: Several endings may be grammatically possible but only one is correct according to the passage.
Extra endings are distractors that mention passage topics but connect them to the wrong subject.
Choosing an ending that is true in general but is not what the passage says about this beginning.
tips: Use grammar to eliminate options first, then decide on meaning.
Each ending is used only once. Cross off used ones.
example: Illustrative: 'Early experiments with the device failed because…' → only endings that start with a reason clause fit (e.g. 'the materials could not withstand high temperatures'). Then check which reason the passage gives.
language: Cause/effect links in the passage: because, owing to, which led to, as a result, consequently

title: Summary completion
summary: Complete a summary of part of the passage, either with words from the passage or with options from a word box.
rule: Find the summary's section, then fill the gaps in order by meaning.

do: Check: words from the passage or a box (A–L)?
Use title + first sentence to find the section
Predict word type and singular / plural
Re-read the finished sentence to check
avoid: Box: words copied from the passage are often traps
Changing the form of a word you copy
Breaking the word limit or misspelling
remember: Box = match meaning; passage = copy exact words

steps: Check the instructions: words FROM THE PASSAGE (with a word limit) or a box of options (A–L)?
Read the summary title and the first sentence to find which section of the passage it covers. A summary usually covers one section, sometimes the whole passage.
For each gap, predict the part of speech (noun / adjective / verb form / number) and whether a noun should be singular or plural.
Find the start of the section and work forward. The gaps are usually in passage order.
Box version: match the meaning, since the options are paraphrases. Passage version: copy the exact word(s).
Read the completed sentence again to check grammar and meaning.
traps: Word box: several options fit grammatically. Only one has the meaning the passage gives. Distractors may be words that appear in the passage.
Passage version: changing the word form (writing 'develop' when the passage has 'development'). Copy the exact form that fits.
Breaking the word limit or adding words that are already printed around the gap.
Misspelling a copied word. It is right there in the passage, so check it letter by letter.
tips: Articles and adjectives before the gap help: 'an ____' → word starting with a vowel sound; 'many ____' → plural noun.
In the practice tests this task appears mostly in Passage 3, so the paraphrasing can be heavy.
example: Summary: 'Zebras tend to live together in small units, which experts call ____.' Passage: '…tracking zebra groups, officially known as harems…' small units ↔ groups, experts call ↔ officially known as → harems.
language: Grammar clues: a/an + singular noun; many/several/a number of + plural noun; to + base verb; the most + adjective

title: Note completion
summary: Fill gaps in notes about the passage with words copied from it, within the word limit.
rule: Copy the exact word(s) from the passage, within the word limit.

do: Read the word limit
Use the note headings to find the section
Predict the answer type (number, name, noun)
Scan in order, copy exactly, re-read the note
avoid: Writing a synonym instead of the passage word
Too many words: pick the key noun
Spelling mistakes when copying
remember: Answers are usually nouns, in passage order

steps: Read the word limit, e.g. 'ONE WORD ONLY' or 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER'.
Use the note headings to find the relevant section of the passage.
Predict the type of each answer (a number, a name, a plural noun, a material, a place).
Scan for the key words around each gap. Answers are usually in passage order.
Copy the word(s) exactly and check that the note reads correctly.
traps: Writing a synonym instead of the passage word. The answer must come from the passage.
Writing too many words because the passage phrase is long. Pick the key noun.
Spelling errors in copied words.
tips: Notes are short, so the grammar is often reduced. Rely on meaning and word type more than on full-sentence grammar.
Answers are usually nouns.
example: Illustrative: Note: 'Used cheap ____ to build the walls' (ONE WORD). Passage: 'the walls were made of inexpensive clay' → clay (cheap ↔ inexpensive).
language: Paraphrase pairs to expect: build ↔ construct, cheap ↔ inexpensive, used for ↔ served as, made of ↔ consisted of

title: Sentence completion
summary: Complete sentences about the passage using words copied from it.
rule: Copy the passage word(s) that complete the sentence correctly.

do: Check the word limit
Underline key words, predict the word type
Scan for the paraphrase (in passage order)
Copy the exact word(s) and re-read
avoid: Wrong word form (adjective instead of noun)
Going over the word limit
A nearby word that doesn't complete the meaning
remember: British or American spelling: both accepted

steps: Check the word limit and whether the answer must come from the passage.
Underline the key words in the sentence and predict the type of word needed.
Scan for the paraphrase of the sentence. Questions follow passage order.
Copy the exact word(s) that complete the sentence grammatically and with the same meaning.
traps: Wrong word form: the gap needs a noun but you copied the adjective or verb from the same phrase.
Exceeding the limit: 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS' → 'the new modern facility' is wrong.
Choosing a nearby word instead of the one that really completes the meaning.
tips: Answers are usually single nouns or short noun phrases (in a course Unit 4 passage: transformation, young age, optimism, skills, negative emotions).
If the passage uses British and American spellings, either is accepted (authorisation / authorization).
example: Sentence: 'Staff need ____ to enter restricted areas.' Passage: 'Do not enter restricted areas without authorization.' → authorisation / authorization.
language: Negative to positive paraphrase: 'not without X' ↔ 'need X'; 'prevented' ↔ 'did not allow'

title: Table completion
summary: Fill gaps in a table that organises information from the passage.
rule: Each gap needs the same type of word as the rest of its column.

do: Read the column and row headings
Check the filled cells in the same column
Find the section; work through it in order
Copy the exact words within the limit
avoid: Following rows when the text goes by columns
Repeating words already in the heading
remember: Usually 1–2 words; numbers in digits are fine

steps: Read the column and row headings. They tell you what kind of information each gap needs.
Look at the completed cells in the same column. Your answer should be the same type (a date, a material, a use).
Find the section of the passage, usually one section read in order, row by row.
Copy the exact words within the word limit.
traps: Reading the table in the wrong direction. Check whether it follows rows or columns as the passage goes.
Repeating information already in the heading (e.g. writing 'year 1850' when the column is 'Year').
tips: Short answers: tables rarely need more than one or two words.
Numbers can be written in digits.
example: Illustrative: Column 'Advantages', row 'Bamboo', other cells: 'lightweight', 'durable' → the gap is an adjective describing a material's strength, e.g. 'flexible'.

title: Flow-chart completion
summary: Complete the stages of a process or sequence of events described in the passage.
rule: Follow the real time order of the process, not the sentence order.

do: Follow the arrows: what happens first, next, last
Find the paragraph(s) that describe the process
Predict each box: a noun or a verb form
Match boxes in order and copy exact words
avoid: 'Before this…': text order ≠ real order
Mixing up the steps before and after the gap

steps: Follow the arrows and understand the sequence before reading. What happens first, next and last?
Find the paragraph that describes the process (often one or two paragraphs).
Predict the word type for each box. Steps are often a noun (a material, a tool) or a verb in a fixed form.
Match each box to the passage in order and copy the exact words.
traps: The passage may describe the steps in a different order than they happen (e.g. 'Before this, …'). Follow the time words, not the sentence order.
Mixing up the step before and after the gap.
tips: Sequence words in the passage locate each stage quickly.
example: Illustrative: Box: 'leaves are ____ in the sun' → passage: 'the leaves are then left to dry outdoors' → dried / dry (check which form fits the box).
language: Sequence words: first, initially, then, next, after that, once, subsequently, before this, finally

title: Diagram labelling
summary: Label the parts of a machine, structure or process shown in a diagram, using words from the passage.
rule: Use the labelled parts as landmarks; copy the noun that names each part.

do: Study the diagram: existing labels and gaps
Find the short section that describes it
Follow the description in order from landmarks
Copy the part's name within the word limit
avoid: Ignoring position words (above, beneath)
Writing a description instead of a name
remember: Answers are nearly always nouns, in order

steps: Study the diagram: identify what is already labelled and where the gaps are.
Find the paragraph(s) that describe the object. It is usually a short section.
Use the labelled parts as landmarks and follow the description in order (top to bottom, inside to outside, start to end).
Copy the noun(s) that name each part, within the word limit.
traps: Labelling the wrong part because you ignored a position word (above, beneath, attached to).
Writing a description instead of the name of the part.
tips: Answers are nearly always nouns copied from the text, in the order of the description.
example: Illustrative: a cross-section of a well with one label missing at the bottom. The text says '…a flight of steps leads down to a pool at the base…'. Use the labelled steps as a landmark, so the bottom label is 'pool'.
language: Position words: above, below, beneath, at the base of, on top of, attached to, inside, surrounding, connected to

title: Multiple choice (one answer)
summary: Choose the one option (A–D) that matches what the passage says.
rule: Answer in your own words first, then pick the option that paraphrases it.

do: Read the stem only; underline its key words
Find the answer place (in passage order)
Form your own answer
Check every option; eliminate the wrong ones
avoid: Options that copy passage words, change meaning
True options that don't answer this question
Extreme words (always, only) vs a cautious text

steps: Read the question stem only (not the options yet) and underline its key words.
Find the part of the passage that answers the stem. Questions follow passage order.
Read that part carefully and form your own answer.
Compare EVERY option with the text. Eliminate those that are false, not mentioned, or answer a different question.
Choose the option that paraphrases the passage's meaning.
traps: Options that copy passage words but change the meaning (wrong subject, wrong time, opposite direction).
An option that is true according to the passage but doesn't answer this question.
Extreme options (always, completely, the only) when the passage is more cautious.
Last question of a set may ask about the whole passage ('the best title', 'the writer's purpose'). Think of the overall message.
tips: In the practice tests most MCQs are in Passage 3. Expect inference and the writer's purpose.
If two options remain, go back to the text and find the exact words that rule one out.
example: Illustrative: Q: 'Why did the project fail?' Option A repeats the passage words 'lack of funding', but the passage says funding was 'never a problem'. The real reason is a paraphrase in option C.
language: Purpose questions: to illustrate, to challenge, to explain, to compare, to argue against
Turn signals near the answer: but, however, although, in reality, contrary to

title: Choose TWO / THREE letters
summary: Choose two or three correct options from a list. Each correct letter scores one mark.
rule: Choose only the options the passage clearly supports for THIS question.

do: Check how many letters and what is asked
Find the paragraph(s) in the passage
Mark each option true / false / not mentioned
Pick only the clearly supported ones
avoid: Mentioned but wrong kind (disadvantage ≠ advantage)
True in real life but not in the passage
remember: Never write more letters than asked

steps: Check how many letters to choose and what the question asks for (which TWO advantages / which TWO statements are true).
Locate the part of the passage. It is often one paragraph, sometimes spread over several.
Check each option against the text and mark it true, false or not mentioned.
Pick only the options the passage clearly supports.
traps: Options that are mentioned but are not what the question asks (a disadvantage when it asks for an advantage).
Options that are true in the real world but not stated in the passage.
tips: The letters can be written in either order.
Each letter is marked separately. If you are sure of one, still guess the other: there is no penalty.
Never write more letters than asked.
example: Illustrative: 'Which TWO benefits of the scheme are mentioned?' If the passage lists costs, safety and speed, but says safety 'has not yet improved', then safety is not a benefit.

title: Short-answer questions
summary: Answer wh-questions about the passage with a few words copied from it.
rule: The question word tells you the answer type; copy only those words.

do: Read the word limit
Underline the question word (what, how many…)
Scan for paraphrased key words, in order
Write only the answer words, copied exactly
avoid: Answering in a full sentence
Too many words for the limit
'Which TWO…': give both, one per box
remember: Numbers and dates can be written in digits

steps: Read the word limit.
Underline the question word (what, which, where, how many, who). It tells you the answer type.
Scan for the paraphrased key words. The answers follow passage order.
Write only the words that answer the question, copied exactly.
traps: Answering in a full sentence. Just give the words.
Writing an answer that is correct but too long for the limit.
'Which TWO…' questions in this format need both items, one in each box.
tips: 'How many / how long / when' → a number or date, which can be written in digits.
example: Illustrative: Q: 'What material was used for the roof?' (ONE WORD) Passage: 'the roof was covered in locally produced slate' → slate.
